case_study_insert.main_stem: Bluewater Laundry & Linen Services (BLL) is a partnership in the consumer services sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2007 by Elena Vasquez, it washes and irons linen for hotel clients along the coast and operates a flat organisational structure with autocratic leadership. BLL plans to invest $420,000 in a high-efficiency industrial washer, financed by $250,000 hire purchase and $170,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $216,000 a year, a variable cost of $8 a unit and a selling price of $26, and processes 20,000 units of laundry a year. BLL faces two problems: a 4% re-wash defect rate, machine downtime of 8% and staff absenteeism of 6%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — March 2025: 4,800 laundry loads were processed; 4% needed re-washing, down from 7% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 51 to 36 per month. Average machine downtime was 6 hours a week. A survey of 200 hotel clients found 70% wanted 24-hour turnaround and 55% would pay $3 more; an operator training session costs $350 per person.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Bluewater Laundry & Linen Services for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.5% to 4.1%, increasing borrowing costs. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% to $13.45 an hour from April 2026, raising wage bills for laundry operatives. (3) Energy and detergent input costs have risen 9.7% year-on-year, while coastal hotel occupancy grew 3.9% and demand for commercial laundry services rose 2.6%.

questions.question_text: BLL plans to finance its new washer with $250,000 hire purchase rather than $170,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for BLL of hire purchase.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the $420,000 washer cost through $250,000 of staged payments, so BLL does not have to pay the full purchase price at once and can keep its $170,000 retained profit as working capital. That reserve is valuable while the 4% re-wash defect rate and 8% machine downtime disrupt the 20,000 units of laundry and the $216,000 fixed costs still have to be met.

Point 2: Hire purchase gives BLL immediate use of the high-efficiency washer while paying for it over time, so the new machine can start reducing the 6 hours a week of downtime straight away. Unlike spending all $170,000 of retained profit, the partnership keeps a cash buffer for the $350 per person operator training and for the 55% of 200 hotel clients who would pay $3 more for better service, letting Elena Vasquez invest in quality while protecting the 20,000 units of laundry at the same time.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to BLL's funding choice, downtime and service.

questions.question_text: BLL wants to win more hotel clients for its new washer capacity. Consider local trade advertising, direct sales visits to hotels, or a social media campaign. Which should BLL choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local trade advertising: Advertisements in hotel-industry magazines or local business papers can reach the 200 hotel clients in BLL's coastal market cheaply and build awareness of the 24-hour turnaround. It is far cheaper than the $420,000 washer, so it protects cash, but readership is passive and untargeted, so it cannot demonstrate the 4% re-wash improvement or win the 55% of clients who would pay $3 more as effectively as a personal approach.

Direct sales visits to hotels: Calling on hotel managers lets BLL show sample linen, explain the lower 4% defect rate and negotiate on the $26 price face to face, which suits a 40-person partnership with a flat structure and autocratic leadership. Visits can target exactly the 70% of surveyed clients wanting 24-hour turnaround and close deals quickly. The drawbacks are travel time and cost per visit, and only a limited number of hotels can be covered by the small sales effort.

Social media campaign: Targeted posts could showcase clean, pressed linen and the faster turnaround to hotel managers, and could highlight the $3 premium service at low cost with measurable responses. It reaches a wider coastal audience than visits and can be run cheaply alongside existing work. However, hotel procurement is often relationship-based, so online leads may be weaker than personal contact, and frequent posting needs staff time that is scarce with 6% absenteeism and 8% downtime.

Recommendation: BLL should choose direct sales visits to hotels. They target the exact 200-client market, demonstrate the quality gains from the $420,000 washer and can convert the 70% demanding 24-hour turnaround into contracts quickly. Trade advertising is rejected as passive and untargeted; social media is rejected as less persuasive for relationship-based hotel buying, though it can support the visits with follow-up messages.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the promotional options with little application to BLL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of BLL with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of BLL with a well-justified recommendation and clear rejection of the alternatives.

questions.question_text: BLL's staff absenteeism is 6%. Explain two benefits for BLL of using autocratic leadership with its 40 staff.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership lets Elena Vasquez set firm, clear rules on attendance and machine operation, which suits the flat organisational structure and can quickly reduce the 6% absenteeism that contributes to 8% machine downtime. With unambiguous instructions, the 4,800 laundry loads can be processed reliably and the 36 monthly complaints kept falling.

Point 2: A directive owner can reassign operatives immediately when the new washer is installed or when an 6% absence occurs, keeping the 20,000 units of laundry on schedule without lengthy consultation. Decisive control also enforces the $350 per person operator training standard, helping cut the 4% re-wash defect rate and protecting the $420,000 investment and the 55% of clients who will pay $3 more for better service. Firm direction also helps BLL honour the 70% demand for 24-hour turnaround among its 200 hotel clients, since one clear rota is easier to enforce when operatives are absent.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to BLL's absenteeism, downtime and defects.

questions.question_text: BLL must cut its 4% re-wash defect rate. Consider end-of-line inspection or a quality assurance programme with the detergent supplier. Which should BLL choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
End-of-line inspection: Checking every load before it leaves the ironer catches badly washed linen and stops the 4% re-wash rate from reaching the 200 hotel clients, directly addressing the 36 complaints. It is under BLL's own control in the flat structure and needs no supplier agreement, which suits Elena Vasquez's autocratic style. Its weakness is that inspection finds faults only after washing, so the 4% has already wasted water and labour, and with 6% absenteeism and 8% downtime there may be few spare staff to inspect every load.

Quality assurance programme with the supplier: Agreeing detergent standards, dosing checks and joint problem-solving attacks the 4% defect rate at source, building on the fall from 7%. It can lower re-wash costs and support the $3 premium for better service, while reducing the need for scarce inspection staff. The limits are that BLL must trust and monitor the supplier, better detergent may raise the $8 variable cost, and results may be slow, which matters while the $420,000 washer is being installed.

Decision: BLL should choose the quality assurance programme with the detergent supplier. Prevention removes the cause of the 4% re-wash rate without tying up 40 staff already affected by 6% absenteeism, and it complements the $350 operator training and the new $420,000 washer. Inspection is rejected as reactive and labour-hungry; a small final spot-check should remain as a safety net while the supplier programme is proven, particularly with 6 hours a week of machine downtime disrupting normal runs at the plant.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two quality approaches with limited application to BLL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of one or both approaches in the context of BLL.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both approaches in the context of BLL with a well-justified decision covering prevention, staffing and cost.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how BLL's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $216,000 ÷ ($26 − $8) = $216,000 ÷ $18 = 12,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 12,000 units of laundry a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $26 − $8 = $18. Answer: contribution per unit is $18.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways BLL's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 12,000-unit break-even output with 20,000 units processed to show a margin of safety of 8,000 loads, indicating how much hotel business BLL can lose before failing to cover the $216,000 fixed costs while the new washer beds in.
2. Use the $18 contribution per unit to evaluate the survey's $3 premium: raising the $26 price to $29 would lift contribution to $21, helping justify the $420,000 washer and the 70% demand for 24-hour turnaround.
3. Use fixed costs and contribution to set the load-volume target needed to meet the $250,000 hire purchase payments, checking that the new machine can be afforded without raising the 4% re-wash rate.
4. Use average total cost ($216,000 ÷ 20,000 units + $8 = $10.80 + $8 = $18.80 a load) and labour productivity (20,000 units ÷ 40 staff = 500 loads per employee) to track the effect of 8% downtime, 6% absenteeism and 9.7% energy inflation on unit costs.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 12,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $18 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 8,000 loads; modelling the $3 premium from $18 contribution; hire-purchase load target for the $250,000 machine; and unit cost $18.80 with productivity 500 loads per employee.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate BLL's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has BLL's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 12.0%
ROCE 2025 = 15.0%

Detailed workings: In 2024 a gross profit of $360,000 on revenue of $900,000 gives 40.0%; in 2025 $495,000 on $1,100,000 gives 45.0%. Operating profit of $108,000 against $900,000 revenue gives 12.0% in 2024, and $165,000 against $1,100,000 gives 15.0% in 2025. Operating profit of $108,000 against capital employed of $900,000 gives 12.0% in 2024, and $165,000 against $1,100,000 gives 15.0% in 2025.

Evaluation: Each measure improved. The gross margin rose from 40.0% to 45.0%, consistent with better control of the 4% re-wash rate and the 36 falling complaints. The operating margin improved from 12.0% to 15.0%, showing the $216,000 fixed costs were spread more effectively as revenue grew by $200,000. The return on capital employed rose from 12.0% to 15.0%, so the extra $200,000 of capital employed was used productively, which supports the $420,000 washer investment. Interest payable increased from $14,000 to $18,000, so the hire purchase has begun to cost more but not enough to offset the gains. A caution is that the 8% machine downtime and 6% absenteeism still constrain the 20,000 units of laundry, and the survey shows only 55% of hotel clients will pay $3 more, so further margin gains may be harder.

Conclusion: BLL's profitability has improved — gross margin, operating margin and return on capital all rose together, and the improvement is not explained by lower finance costs. Management should protect the 45.0% gross margin against 9.7% energy inflation and use the new washer to cut downtime, so the 15.0% return is maintained.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three profitability ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation and a justified conclusion on whether profitability improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for BLL of offering the 24-hour turnaround wanted by 70% of surveyed hotel clients.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey of 200 hotel clients shows 70% want 24-hour turnaround and 55% would pay $3 more, so BLL can charge $29 instead of $26 for express loads, lifting the $18 contribution per unit and helping fund the $420,000 washer and the $250,000 hire purchase. Faster service also makes BLL more competitive for the 2.6% growth in laundry demand and cuts the 36 monthly complaints.

Disadvantage: Guaranteeing 24 hours may be hard while 8% machine downtime and 6% absenteeism persist, and extra shifts would add wage costs that the insert does not quantify, possibly erasing the $3 premium. Rushing the 4,800 loads could also raise the 4% re-wash defect rate, and the $350 operator training needed for the new washer may take staff away from the express service. Processing 4,800 loads in a quarter already stretches a 40-person team, so an unconditional 24-hour promise could raise downtime as machines are pushed harder.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to BLL's survey, downtime and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.1%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.7% rise in energy and detergent costs will affect BLL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.5% to 4.1%): With $250,000 of hire purchase, a 0.6 percentage-point rise would add roughly 0.006 × $250,000 = $1,500 a year if the agreement is interest-rate linked, small beside the $216,000 fixed costs and likely already fixed in the hire-purchase terms. The $170,000 retained profit carries no interest at all. Higher rates may dampen hotel investment, but the direct cash effect on BLL is modest.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $13.45 an hour): With a workforce of 40, this raises the wage bill for operatives and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no annual total can honestly be invented; the defensible check is productivity of 20,000 units ÷ 40 staff = 500 loads per employee. With $18 contribution per unit, the rise is absorbable while downtime stays at 8% and absenteeism at 6%; if those worsen, unit labour costs climb quickly.

Energy and detergent inflation (9.7%): The insert does not split the $8 variable cost, so only a bound can be shown: if the whole $8 rose 9.7%, that is 0.097 × $8 = $0.78 per load, or about $15,440 a year at 20,000 loads, cutting contribution from $18 toward $17.22. Hotel occupancy growing 3.9% and laundry demand 2.6% may allow BLL to pass some of this on, and the new high-efficiency washer should lower energy use, but the 4% re-wash rate wastes energy as well.

Conclusion: The 9.7% rise in energy and detergent costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 20,000 loads, directly erodes the $18 contribution that funds the $420,000 washer, and is amplified by the 4% re-wash rate. The interest-rate effect is small and largely fixed; the wage rise is manageable at 500 loads per employee, whereas energy inflation raises the cost of every single load and cannot be avoided.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to BLL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on BLL's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of BLL with a well-justified greatest-impact judgement and reasons for rejecting the others.
